title: Europe’s Ancient Landscapes May Have Been More Open Than We Thought
paragraphs: The notion that primeval Europe was one unbroken, shadowy wildwood is a stubborn one, and a new synthesis from Aarhus University in Denmark seeks to dislodge it. Rather than staking its case on a single record, the team braided together fossil pollen and plant remains, charcoal from ancient wildfires, isotopic and chemical signatures in the teeth and bones of herbivores, fossil insects and mammals, and environmental DNA preserved in sediments.

What emerges is a continent that, for well over 20 million years, was governed not by closed canopy but by a shifting patchwork of trees, clearings and flowering plants, a pattern that persisted in temperate conditions akin to today’s as well as in hotter and colder spells. The authors place large herbivores, among them elephants, rhinoceroses, aurochs and bison, at the heart of this account: by grazing and trampling, they held back the vegetation that would otherwise have closed in.

The argument is not merely academic. Senior author Jens-Christian Svenning contends that current reforestation practices are “on the wrong track”, singling out schemes, such as Danish subsidies, that reward only dense forest planting, and the team advocates restoring woodland-grassland mosaics and their large grazers instead. Caution is nonetheless in order: a synthesis of the fossil record inevitably contends with patchy evidence, no single proxy tells the whole tale, and other specialists may read the same records differently. The paper appears in Biological Conservation.

questions.q: What does the team propose instead of dense forest planting?
questions.a: Restoring woodland-grassland mosaics and large grazers.
The vegetation closing in to form dense canopy.

questions.q: What caution do the authors’ critics or readers need to keep in mind?
questions.a: The fossil evidence is patchy and other specialists may read it differently.
